blocks.x: In the heyday of Lost, The 4400 was a series that was just as deserving of attention. The high concept was unlike anything else on television and was set up perfectly for appointment viewing. When the titular 4400 arrive in a mysterious ball of light, Tom Baldwin (Joel Gretsch) and Diana Skouris (Jacqueline McKenzie) are tasked with investigating the circumstances of these arrivals. Each person who appears in the same spot in Washington has not aged a day since their abduction, and some have even developed supernatural abilities.

The mystery of how and why powers the series in a fascinating mystery that gets better and better. Each episode follows Homeland Security’s attempt to unravel the enigma of these returnees. Extremely character-driven, The 4400 explores the specifics of many of the abductees.

Mahershala Ali’s character, Richard Tyler, was a pilot in the Korean War who had fallen in love with a white woman. Racial tensions were high when he was abducted and returned to the present day. Decades later, the granddaughter of his lover, Lily (Laura Allen), is also abducted and returns pregnant with his child. The first season seeks to uncover exactly why these people were abducted and the truth behind their abilities.

The 4400 plays with the idea of alien abduction only to reveal that these people weren’t taken by extraterrestrials, but humans from the future. This twist deepens the intrigue even further in typical puzzlebox mystery fashion. These humans had sent the abductees to this time in order to avert some sort of ambiguous catastrophe.

Each season of the perfect Manifest replacement show escalates the stakes of the previous, a rarity for high-concept sci-fi series such as this. The heart of the narrative, however, is the characters. Once the main mystery is solved, The 4400 explores the ramifications of what people with such power are able to do. Tragically, the 2008 Writers’ Strike took another victim. Like so many other inventive series of the time, the show fell to the sword. Only heavy-hitters such as Lost and Breaking Bad survived, while other deserving stories were cancelled. Despite all, The 4400 delivered four solid seasons. Though it ends on a cliffhanger, none of the episodes leave viewers wanting.
